y-m-67-01.topic: Limit of a sequence: the form of a difference of two infinities (irrational expressions)
y-m-67-01.goal: In the limit of a sequence given by an irrational expression, learn that the fact that both values grow does not by itself fix the difference, and check the limit by either numerical values or transforming the expression.
y-m-67-01.material: For a natural number n, let a_n = √(n²+n) − n. (Read as: square root of n squared plus n, minus n. lim, n→∞ means "the limit as n grows without bound.") Hayun solved lim a_n as below.
y-m-67-01.thinking.0: Find the first line in the solution that goes wrong
y-m-67-01.thinking.1: Read a numerical table as evidence for a candidate value while keeping it apart from proof
y-m-67-01.thinking.2: Explain an error to another person with solid reasons
y-m-67-01.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-01.prereq.1: The meaning of convergence and divergence of a sequence, and reading the limit symbol lim
y-m-67-01.prereq.2: Calculating expressions with square roots (a calculator may be used)
y-m-67-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Hayun's solution where the logic is wrong. (A line whose conclusion is wrong is also accepted, but look for the line that is the cause of the mistake.)
y-m-67-01.s.s1.hint.0: Ask one by one whether each line must follow from the line just before it.
y-m-67-01.s.s1.line.1: As n grows without bound, both √(n²+n) and n grow without bound.
y-m-67-01.s.s1.line.2: Both values grow without bound, so their difference converges to ∞−∞ = 0.
y-m-67-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. When both values grow without bound, their difference can be 0, can be some other number, or can grow without bound, so "∞−∞" is a form whose value is not determined. The fact in line 2 alone does not tell you the difference. The conclusion in line 4 depends on line 3.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.prompt: When a_n was calculated for n=10, 100, 1000, 10000, it came to about 0.4881, 0.4988, 0.49988, 0.49999. Which is the most fitting judgment you can make about lim a_n from this table?
y-m-67-01.s.s2.hint.0: First say whether the values in the table are getting larger or smaller.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate how the difference from 0.5 changes each time n is made 10 times as large.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.o.d: Nothing can be said from the table alone. You need to calculate more.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.r.d: If you do not use the regularity of the table (the tendency of the values to approach one number) as evidence, you start without even a candidate value.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.explain: The values in the table do not shrink toward 0 but grow toward 0.5. So the "∞−∞=0" in line 3 is wrong for this sequence. However, the table has only a finite number of values, so it is evidence that offers a candidate, not a proof.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.acc.0: The caution that a table is not a proof is valid. But the table is also evidence pointing to the candidate value 0.5, so stating a candidate and then finding a way to check it goes one step further.
y-m-67-01.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to send to Hayun. Include the limit (or the candidate value), how you checked it, and why "both numbers grow, so the difference is 0" does not work. You may choose either a numerical table or transforming the expression as the way to check.
y-m-67-01.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate the values of a_n yourself at n=1000 and 10000, and say which number they stick to.
y-m-67-01.s.s3.hint.1: If you use only a table, think about whether you can add the one sentence "this is a guess, not a proof."
y-m-67-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my reply contain both the limit (or the candidate value) and its reasons?
y-m-67-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I explain that the fact "both grow" and the conclusion "the difference is 0" are separate?
y-m-67-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I tell apart whether the reason I wrote is a proof or evidence that shows a candidate?
y-m-67-01.s.s3.model.0: That solution is wrong. Even if both numbers grow without bound, the difference does not become 0. If n=100, √10100≈100.4988, so a_100≈0.4988, and if n=10000, it is about 0.49999. So it looks like it gets close to 1/2. You must not say right away that ∞−∞ is 0.
y-m-67-01.s.s3.model.1: Rewrite a_n as n/(√(n²+n)+n) and divide the numerator and denominator by n to get 1/(√(1+1/n)+1), so the limit is 1/2. Even though both numbers grow, the difference went to 1/2, not 0. ∞−∞ is a form whose value depends on the situation, so you must not fix it as 0.
y-m-67-01.title: Checking a Solution for the Limit of √(n²+n) − n
y-m-67-01.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate directly the difference between √(n²+n) and n at n=10 and n=100, and compare it with the claim in each line.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.o.a: It seems to converge toward 0.5, but a proof is needed separately.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.r.a: You read the table as evidence suggesting a candidate value, while keeping it separate from a proof.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.o.b: It can be seen to converge to 0. This is because the two numbers become similar.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.r.b: The values in the table do not shrink to 0 but rather grow toward 0.5. The feeling that "they become similar" is a separate matter from "the difference is 0".
y-m-67-01.s.s2.o.c: It can be seen to diverge. This is because the value changes with each n.
y-m-67-01.s.s2.r.c: The value changing is different from diverging. You need to look at how the size of the changes varies.

y-m-67-02.title: How does the limit change when r changes?
y-m-67-02.topic: Limit of a sequence: fractions with the geometric sequence rⁿ and the range of r
y-m-67-02.goal: Using the fact that the behavior of rⁿ depends on the value of r, make several values of r that give the same limit, and explain what happens at the boundary values (r=1, r=−1).
y-m-67-02.material: For a real number r, consider the sequence a_n = (rⁿ⁺¹ + 3)/(rⁿ + 1) (n=1, 2, 3, …). (rⁿ means "r to the power n.") If even one term has a denominator of 0, the sequence is treated as not defined for that r. Look at how the limit changes with the value of r.
y-m-67-02.thinking.0: Make examples that meet the condition yourself
y-m-67-02.thinking.2: Work out whether the limit is defined at the boundary values
y-m-67-02.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-02.prereq.1: The step of finding the limit of the geometric sequence rⁿ (|r|<1, r=1, r>1, and so on)
y-m-67-02.prereq.2: Calculations that simplify a fraction by dividing
y-m-67-02.s.s1.prompt: What is lim a_n when r=2?
y-m-67-02.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate a_n for n=1, 2, 5, 20, make a table, and see which value it gets close to.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.hint.1: For large n, compare which term in the numerator and denominator has the greatest influence on the value.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.o.a: It is 3. This is because only the constant term 3 in the numerator is left.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.r.a: This ignored the effect of 2ⁿ growing without bound and looked only at the constant term.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.explain: Dividing the numerator and denominator by 2ⁿ gives (2+3/2ⁿ)/(1+1/2ⁿ), and as n grows it gets close to 2/1=2.
y-m-67-02.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different values of r for which the limit is 3 and enter them. (r is a real number and may be written as a decimal. a_n must be defined for every n.)
y-m-67-02.s.s2.hint.1: Split r into those where rⁿ gets close to 0, those where it grows without bound, and those where its size does not change.
y-m-67-02.s.s2.ok.c1: No term has a denominator of 0.
y-m-67-02.s.s2.fail.c1: If r=−1, the denominator (−1)ⁿ+1 is 0 when n is odd.
y-m-67-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The limit is 3 at this r.
y-m-67-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The limit is not 3 at this r (it is another value or does not exist).
y-m-67-02.s.s2.explain: If |r|<1, rⁿ→0, so the limit is 3/1=3. Surprisingly, r=3 also has limit 3. This is because when r>1 the limit is r itself. If r=1 every term is 2, if r=−1 it is not defined, and if r<−1 the limit is r.
y-m-67-02.s.s3.prompt: Explain in one sentence each what happens to a_n when r=1 and when r=−1.
y-m-67-02.s.s3.hint.0: Put r=1 into the expression and calculate a_n for n=1, 2, 3.
y-m-67-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put in r=−1 and calculate the denominator when n is odd and when n is even.
y-m-67-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you avoid swapping the explanations for r=1 and r=−1?
y-m-67-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: For r=−1, did you tell apart "there is no limit" from "the sequence is not defined"?
y-m-67-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check the values you wrote using the first few terms yourself?
y-m-67-02.s.s3.model.0: If r=1, every term is 4/2=2, so the limit is 2, not 3. If r=−1, the denominator (−1)ⁿ+1 is 0 when n is odd, so that term is not defined and the sequence itself does not exist.
y-m-67-02.s.s3.model.1: If r is 1, the limit is 2, and if r is −1, you would divide by 0 at the odd-numbered terms, so it is not defined and you cannot talk about a limit.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.o.b: It is 2. This is because the ratio of the largest terms remains.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.r.b: You looked at the ratio of the terms that grow the most in the numerator and the denominator.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.o.c: It is 7/3. This is because that is the value at n=1.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.r.c: You mistook the value of the first term for the limit. The limit is about the behavior as n grows.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.o.d: It diverges. This is because both the numerator and the denominator grow.
y-m-67-02.s.s1.r.d: Even if both the numerator and the denominator grow, their ratio can approach a single number.
y-m-67-02.s.s2.hint.0: Put in various values of r (positive and negative, smaller and larger than 1) and compare the first few terms of a_n with the values near n=20.

y-m-67-03.title: If the terms get close to 0, does the sum stop too?
y-m-67-03.topic: Limit of a sequence: convergence of a series and the limit of its terms
y-m-67-03.goal: Adjust your judgment while reading a table of partial sums of a series whose terms go to 0, tell apart the limits of the table from the role of a grouping argument, and write a counterexample yourself.
y-m-67-03.material: That a series Σ aₙ (from n=1 without end; read as: sigma a n) converges means that the partial sum S_N = a₁ + a₂ + … + a_N gets close to one number as N→∞. Minjun said, "If the term aₙ gets close to 0, then the series Σ aₙ converges too." Let's evaluate this statement while looking at the data one piece at a time.
y-m-67-03.thinking.0: Recognize the risk of generalizing from a few examples
y-m-67-03.thinking.1: Tell apart the roles of numerical evidence and proof
y-m-67-03.thinking.2: Make a counterexample yourself and explain it
y-m-67-03.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-03.prereq.1: That the series Σ a_n is defined as the limit of the partial sums S_N = a₁+…+a_N
y-m-67-03.prereq.2: The experience of seeing for yourself a case where a geometric series converges
y-m-67-03.s.s1.prompt: Follow how my judgment about Minjun's statement changes with the data.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, tell apart whether what I changed is the judgment or the degree of confidence.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare directly, using the numbers in the table, how S_N grows as N gets larger.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Example ①: if aₙ = 1/2ⁿ, then S₁₀ = 1 − 1/2¹⁰ ≈ 0.99902, which gets close to 1. Example ②: if aₙ = 1/n², then S₁₀₀₀ ≈ 1.6439, and it is known to stop near 1.645 even if you go further. In both cases aₙ → 0 and the series converges.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is your judgment now about Minjun's statement?
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.after: The two examples only give it some plausibility. A claim of "always" can be broken by a single counterexample, so an example that goes to 0 more slowly is important.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is probably true. Both examples held.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Were you aware that your grounds are only two examples when you judged? A claim of "always" must be tested with more different examples.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Hold back judgment, and also test an example that goes to 0 more slowly.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that saw that the conclusion can change depending on what kind of examples they are.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is false. This is because there are only two examples.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Having few examples is not a reason for deciding true or false; it means the grounds are weak.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Example ③: if aₙ = 1/n, then aₙ → 0. The partial sums are S₁₀ ≈ 2.929, S₁₀₀ ≈ 5.187, S₁₀₀₀ ≈ 7.485, S₁₀⁴ ≈ 9.788, S₁₀⁵ ≈ 12.090, S₁₀⁶ ≈ 14.393. Each time N is made 10 times as large, it grows by about 2.3.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: How does this table affect Minjun's statement?
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.after: If it keeps growing steadily by about 2.3 each 10-fold step, the sum may grow without bound. But the table cannot guarantee anything beyond the millionth term.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It still seems it will converge. This is because the increase is not large.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The increase looking small and the increase stopping are different. Look at whether the increase stays constant.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is likely to diverge. It keeps growing by a similar amount every 10-fold step.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This read the pattern where the size of the increase stays constant as evidence.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: I cannot be certain, but my suspicion has grown. More checking is needed.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This reflected the evidence while knowing the limit that the table has only a finite number of values.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Let's compare by grouping. In 1 + 1/2 + (1/3+1/4) + (1/5+1/6+1/7+1/8) + (1/9+…+1/16) + …, each bracket has a sum of at least 1/2. (For example, 1/3+1/4 ≥ 2×(1/4) = 1/2, and 1/5+…+1/8 ≥ 4×(1/8) = 1/2.) Therefore S_(2ᵏ) ≥ 1 + k/2.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How is this argument related to the earlier table?
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.after: aₙ=1/n gets close to 0, but the partial sums grow without bound. So Minjun's statement does not hold in general. aₙ→0 is only a necessary condition for a series to converge, not a sufficient one.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It does not replace the table. It holds only when k is small.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The inequality holds for every natural number k. See whether there is any evidence that it holds only for some k.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It shows that the table was wrong. The sum stops at 14.4.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The values in the table keep getting larger as N grows. There is no evidence anywhere that it stops at 14.4.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It turns the suspicion from the table into a proof. The sum grows without bound.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This confirmed the trend that the numerical table showed with an argument for all k.
y-m-67-03.s.s1.reflect: How did your judgment, which at first felt "probably true," change as you met the slowly shrinking example and the grouping argument? What did the numerical table and the argument each do for you?
y-m-67-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain to Minjun with a counterexample. Include which sequence aₙ you use and the reason the series does not converge even though aₙ → 0 (what happens to the partial sums). It is even better if you use a counterexample other than 1/n.
y-m-67-03.s.s2.hint.0: Read again how much the partial sum of 1/n grew when N was made 10 times as large in the table.
y-m-67-03.s.s2.hint.1: To break Minjun's statement, you need just one sequence whose terms go to 0 and whose partial sums do not gather at one number. Choose one candidate.
y-m-67-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check for yourself that the sequence you gave gets close to 0?
y-m-67-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write, even in one sentence, why the partial sums grow without bound?
y-m-67-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you write knowing that "one example is enough"?
y-m-67-03.s.s2.model.0: If aₙ = 1/n, then aₙ → 0, but the partial sums satisfy S_(2ᵏ) ≥ 1 + k/2, so they grow without bound and diverge. So even if the terms go to 0, you cannot say the series converges.
y-m-67-03.s.s2.model.1: If aₙ = 1/√n, it gets close to 0, but 1/√n ≥ 1/n, so the partial sums are not smaller than the partial sums of 1/n and keep growing. The partial sums grow without bound, so it diverges.

y-m-67-04.title: Can we name the slope of the tangent line as a single value?
y-m-67-04.topic: Various differentiation methods: implicit differentiation and sufficiency of conditions
y-m-67-04.goal: Learn that on a curve given implicitly, one x-coordinate can correspond to several points, and explain by telling apart points where the slope of the tangent line is 0 and points where the slope formula is not defined.
y-m-67-04.material: Curve C: x² + xy + y² = 3 (x and y are real numbers). Soeun differentiated both sides with respect to x and got dy/dx = −(2x+y)/(x+2y) (where x+2y≠0). (Read dy/dx as: dy dx.) The homework problem is: "When the x-coordinate of a point P on C is 1, find the slope of the tangent line at P."
y-m-67-04.thinking.0: Decide whether the information is sufficient
y-m-67-04.thinking.1: Make examples that meet the condition
y-m-67-04.thinking.2: Tell apart an expression not being defined from there being no tangent line
y-m-67-04.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-04.prereq.1: The experience of having done implicit differentiation (seeing y as a function of x and differentiating both sides with respect to x) at least once
y-m-67-04.s.s1.prompt: What more do you need to know to fix the answer to this problem as a single value?
y-m-67-04.s.s1.hint.1: For each point you get, calculate dy/dx separately and compare whether they are equal.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.explain: Putting x=1 into the equation of the curve gives y²+y−2=0, that is, (y+2)(y−1)=0, so y=1 or y=−2. There are two points, so the slope must also be found separately for each point.
y-m-67-04.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different points on C, with integer coordinates, where the tangent line is parallel to the x-axis, and enter (x, y).
y-m-67-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think about which of the numerator and the denominator of the dy/dx expression must have what value for the slope to be 0.
y-m-67-04.s.s2.hint.1: Once you choose a candidate point, put it into the equation of the curve and calculate to check that it really is on the curve.
y-m-67-04.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a point on C.
y-m-67-04.s.s2.fail.c1: It is not a point on the curve x²+xy+y²=3.
y-m-67-04.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a point where Soeun's slope formula can be used.
y-m-67-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The denominator x+2y is 0, so Soeun's formula cannot be used at this point.
y-m-67-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The slope of the tangent line at this point is not 0.
y-m-67-04.s.s2.explain: For dy/dx = 0, the numerator 2x+y must be 0, that is, y=−2x. Putting this into the curve gives 3x²=3, so x=±1 and the points are (1, −2) and (−1, 2). Of the two points from step 1, the slope is 0 at (1, −2) and −1 at (1, 1), so the answer differs unless the point is fixed.
y-m-67-04.s.s3.prompt: The point (2, −1) is on C (4−2+1=3). At this point x+2y=0, so Soeun's formula cannot be used. May we say "there is no tangent line at this point"? If there is a tangent line, write what line it is and why you judge so.
y-m-67-04.s.s3.hint.0: Put (2, −1) into the dy/dx expression and calculate the numerator and denominator separately.
y-m-67-04.s.s3.hint.1: Swap the roles of x and y and think about dx/dy, and check what its value is at the same point.
y-m-67-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write "the slope formula cannot be used" and "there is no tangent line" as separate things?
y-m-67-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is your judgment one made while imagining what shape the curve has near this point?
y-m-67-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you try thinking with the roles of x and y swapped?
y-m-67-04.s.s3.model.0: There is a tangent line. When the denominator is 0 you just cannot use the dy/dx expression, and at that point the curve stands vertically, so the tangent line is the vertical line x=2. The numerator −(2x+y)=−3 is not 0, so this is the case where the slope grows without bound.
y-m-67-04.s.s3.model.1: You must not say there is no tangent line. Seeing x as an expression in y and finding dx/dy gives −(x+2y)/(2x+y)=0, so it is the vertical tangent line x=2 along which x does not change. The slope is just not defined.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think directly about whether the condition given in the problem, "the x-coordinate is 1", alone determines a single point on the curve.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.o.a: Nothing more is needed. If x=1, the curve determines y as well, as a single value.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.r.a: You missed that on a curve given implicitly, one x can correspond to several values of y.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.o.b: A figure showing the shape of the graph of C is needed.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.r.b: A figure helps, but the number of points can be checked from the equation alone.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.o.c: The y-coordinate of P (check that there is only one point with x=1)
y-m-67-04.s.s1.r.c: You saw that you must first check whether the point is determined uniquely.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.o.d: The value of d²y/dx² is needed.
y-m-67-04.s.s1.r.d: The slope is determined by the first derivative. The second derivative is an issue only after the point is determined.

y-m-67-05.title: For what a does aˣ have slope 1 at x=0?
y-m-67-05.topic: Various differentiation methods: the derivative of an exponential function and the constant e
y-m-67-05.goal: Test a memorized differentiation formula with numbers, narrow down the range of a with m(a)=1 using a table, and connect that this value is e and that (aˣ)′ = aˣ ln a.
y-m-67-05.material: Let m(a) be the derivative at x=0 of the exponential function f(x) = aˣ (a>0, a≠1). By the definition, m(a) is the value that (aʰ−1)/h gets close to when h is near 0. All the values below are approximations calculated with h=0.000001.
y-m-67-05.thinking.1: Narrow the range with a numerical table
y-m-67-05.thinking.2: Explain numbers with the definition and an expression
y-m-67-05.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-05.prereq.1: The definition of the derivative f′(0) = lim (f(h)−f(0))/h
y-m-67-05.prereq.2: That the graph of the exponential function aˣ is smooth
y-m-67-05.s.s1.prompt: Subin memorized (aˣ)′ = x·aˣ⁻¹. Putting x=0 into this formula gives m(a)=0. But when a=2, (2ʰ−1)/h is about 0.718, 0.696, 0.693 at h=0.1, 0.01, 0.001. How would you judge Subin's formula?
y-m-67-05.s.s1.hint.0: Read from the change in the numbers where the value goes as h shrinks to 0.1, 0.01, 0.001.
y-m-67-05.s.s1.hint.1: Put the value from putting x=0 into Subin's formula side by side with the values in the table and compare them.
y-m-67-05.s.s1.o.a: 0.693 is close to 0, so Subin's formula can be considered right.
y-m-67-05.s.s1.r.a: Did you see the tendency that even when h is reduced, the value does not go to 0 but stays near 0.693?
y-m-67-05.s.s1.o.b: The values in the table stay near 0.69, so this formula is not right.
y-m-67-05.s.s1.r.b: You read as evidence that when h is reduced, the value sticks to some positive number rather than 0.
y-m-67-05.s.s1.o.c: h is not 0, so the table has no meaning, and we should trust the memorized formula.
y-m-67-05.s.s1.r.c: The derivative is exactly the value when h gets close to 0. The table is evidence heading toward that value.
y-m-67-05.s.s1.explain: Even when h is reduced, the value gathers near 0.693, not 0. So at x=0, Subin's formula x·aˣ⁻¹ = 0 does not match the slope of the tangent line for a=2.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.prompt: Go looking for the a with m(a)=1. Check your judgment while looking at the data one piece at a time.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.hint.0: At each step, say in one line whether the new data supports or refutes your guess.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.hint.1: Put the value in the table and the value of ln a side by side at the same a and compare how large the difference is.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.info: m(2) ≈ 0.693, m(3) ≈ 1.099, m(4) ≈ 1.386. As a gets larger, m(a) gets larger too.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.ask: Roughly where is the a with m(a)=1?
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.after: m(2)<1<m(3), so the answer is between 2 and 3. But which side it is closer to is still a guess.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.o.a: Less than 2. This is because m(2) is already close to 1.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.r.a: m(2)≈0.693 falls short of 1. As a gets larger m gets larger, so to reach 1 shouldn't it be greater than 2?
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.o.b: Between 2 and 3, and it looks closer to 3.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that used the fact that 1 is closer to 1.099 than to 0.693.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.o.c: Between 3 and 4. This is because m(3) still falls short of 1.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.r.c: m(3)≈1.099 has already passed 1. Look at where it first goes beyond 1.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.o.d: All you can say is that it is between 2 and 3.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.0.r.d: This is a cautious judgment that, with only three points, you do not know the exact position.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.1.after: m(2.7)<1<m(2.8), so the answer looks to be between 2.7 and 2.8. The exact value cannot be fixed with a table.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.1.o.a: a=2.75 is exactly the answer, in the very middle of 2.7 and 2.8.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.1.r.a: This asserted that a value not in the table is exact. You have to check the actual value of m at 2.75.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.1.o.b: It looks to be between 2.7 and 2.8, but the exact value cannot be fixed with a table.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.1.r.b: This narrowed the range while admitting the limit of the table.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.1.o.c: The value that is exactly 1 is not in the table, so no such a exists.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.1.r.c: m(a) changes continuously with a, so a value not in the table does not mean it does not exist.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.info: The number for which m(a)=1 is called e, and e ≈ 2.71828…. Also m(a) = ln a (the natural logarithm of a), and so (aˣ)′ = aˣ ln a. Compared with the table, ln 2 ≈ 0.693, ln 3 ≈ 1.099, ln 2.7 ≈ 0.993.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.ask: How does Subin's original formula compare with this result?
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.after: At x=0, Subin's formula is always 0, but the actual slope is ln a. If a≠1, then ln a≠0, so Subin's formula is wrong. m(a)=1 is when ln a=1, that is, a=e.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.o.a: Subin's formula can be considered right at x=0 only when a=e.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.r.a: If a=e then m=1, but Subin's formula gives 0 at x=0. Check whether it is still right.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.o.b: The values in the table being similar to the values of ln a is just a coincidence.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.r.b: It is hard to see it as a coincidence that all three values agree up to the third decimal place.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.o.c: At x=0, Subin's formula gives 0 and the actual value is ln a (≠0), so the formula is wrong.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.st.2.r.c: You confirmed with an expression the mismatch that the numerical table showed.
y-m-67-05.s.s2.reflect: The order was: at first trusting the memorized formula, refuting it with numbers, narrowing the range with the table, and then the definition (e) and the expression explaining the table. At which step did your confidence change? How is what the table did different from what the expression did?

y-m-67-06.title: Checking a solution that found the slope of an inverse function
y-m-67-06.topic: Various differentiation methods: differentiating an inverse function
y-m-67-06.goal: Correct at which point f′ should be calculated when finding the derivative of an inverse function, and decide for which functions Seoyun's formula happens to be right by coincidence.
y-m-67-06.thinking.0: Find the line in the solution that goes wrong
y-m-67-06.thinking.1: Explain the cause of the error and fix it
y-m-67-06.thinking.2: Find the condition under which a formula happens to be right
y-m-67-06.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-06.prereq.1: The meaning of an inverse function (if f(a)=b then g(b)=a)
y-m-67-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Seoyun's solution where the logic is wrong. (The line that is the cause is best, but the conclusion line is also accepted.)
y-m-67-06.s.s1.hint.1: For the pair g(x) = ln x and f(x) = eˣ, find g′(1) and 1/f′(1) and compare them with Seoyun's formula.
y-m-67-06.s.s1.line.0: f(x) = x³ + x and g is the inverse function of f. Find g′(2).
y-m-67-06.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. The input of f that corresponds to the input 2 of g is not 2 but the a with f(a)=2 (that is, g(2)). The calculation in line 3 itself is right, but it is a value at the wrong point, and so the result in line 4 cannot be trusted either.
y-m-67-06.s.s2.prompt: Write a message to send to Seoyun. Include the correct value of g′(2) and what needs to be fixed in Seoyun's formula.
y-m-67-06.s.s2.hint.0: First find the x for which f(x)=2 (checking by substitution is fine).
y-m-67-06.s.s2.hint.1: Once g(2) is fixed, calculate the slope of f at that point and put it into Seoyun's formula.
y-m-67-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Besides the correct value, did you explain why the point where f′ is calculated is 1?
y-m-67-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write the wrong line and the fix separately so that Seoyun can understand?
y-m-67-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check the value you wrote with something like f(1)=2?
y-m-67-06.s.s2.model.0: g′(2)=1/4. f(1)=2, so g(2)=1, and g′(2)=1/f′(g(2))=1/f′(1)=1/4. The point where you should find f′ is not 2 but g(2)=1.
y-m-67-06.s.s2.model.1: The answer is one fourth. The input where the inverse function gives 2 is x=1, so I used the slope of f at that point, 4, to get 1/4. You must not put 2 in as it is, as in 1/f′(2).
y-m-67-06.s.s3.prompt: For which function is Seoyun's formula g′(x) = 1/f′(x) right even when used as it is at every x?
y-m-67-06.s.s3.hint.0: First sort out whether the f′ of each function depends on x.
y-m-67-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare g′(2) and 1/f′(2) directly at one point (for example x=2).
y-m-67-06.s.s3.explain: If f′ is constant, f′ is the same wherever you measure it, so Seoyun's formula happens to be right. If f(x)=4x−1, then g(x)=(x+1)/4 and g′=1/4=1/f′. If f′ differs from point to point, the same mistake shows up in the value.
y-m-67-06.material: The function f(x) = x³ + x (x is any real number) is one-to-one, so it has an inverse function g. (g′(2) is read as "g prime of two" and means the derivative of the inverse function g at x=2.) Seoyun found g′(2) as shown below. For the inverse function g, f(g(x)) = x holds for all x.
y-m-67-06.prereq.3: Differentiation of composite functions (chain rule): differentiating both sides of f(g(x)) = x gives the relation between g′(x) and f′.
y-m-67-06.s.s1.hint.0: Mark whether the numbers 2 and 13 written in each line are inputs of g or inputs of f.
y-m-67-06.s.s3.r.a: f′ is a function whose value differs with x. For such a function, putting in the wrong point changes the value.
y-m-67-06.s.s3.r.b: If g(x) = √(x−1), then g′(2) = 1/2 and 1/f′(2) = 1/4, which differ.
y-m-67-06.s.s3.r.c: You used the fact that f′ is the same everywhere.
y-m-67-06.s.s3.r.d: If g(x) = ln x, then g′(x) = 1/x and 1/f′(x) = e⁻ˣ, which differ.

y-m-67-07.title: Does the shape of the curve change at a point where the second derivative is 0?
y-m-67-07.topic: Various differentiation methods: the second derivative and inflection points
y-m-67-07.goal: Show with a counterexample that the condition f″(a)=0 alone does not make a point an inflection point, and say for yourself what to check for it to be an inflection point.
y-m-67-07.material:
Consider the function f(x) = xⁿ (n is a natural number that is at least 3). The second derivative is f″(x) = n(n−1)xⁿ⁻² and f″(0) = 0. (Read f″ as: f double prime.) An inflection point is a point where the curve changes between concave and convex, that is, a point where the sign of f″ changes. Dohyun said, "If f″(a) = 0, then (a, f(a)) is an inflection point." The table below shows the values of f″(−1), f″(0), f″(1).

| n | f″(−1) | f″(0) | f″(1) |
| 3 | −6 | 0 | 6 |
| 4 | 12 | 0 | 12 |
| 5 | −20 | 0 | 20 |
| 6 | 30 | 0 | 30 |
y-m-67-07.thinking.0: Read the pattern in the table
y-m-67-07.thinking.2: Tell apart sufficient and necessary conditions
y-m-67-07.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-07.prereq.1: The relationship between the sign of the second derivative and a curve being concave or convex
y-m-67-07.s.s1.prompt: If you evaluate Dohyun's statement using the table as evidence, what do you get?
y-m-67-07.s.s1.hint.0: In each row, read in order the signs of f″ at x=−1, 0, 1.
y-m-67-07.s.s1.hint.1: Separate the rows where the signs on both sides of the point where f″ is 0 are the same from the rows where they are different.
y-m-67-07.s.s1.o.a: It is true. All four functions have f″=0 at x=0, so it holds.
y-m-67-07.s.s1.r.a: f″=0 is only one condition for an inflection point. Did you also read the signs on both sides of that point?
y-m-67-07.s.s1.o.b: We cannot know. Four examples cannot give a general conclusion.
y-m-67-07.s.s1.r.b: A claim that "it always holds" can be broken by even a single counterexample. What matters is the existence of a counterexample, not the number of examples.
y-m-67-07.s.s1.o.c: It is false. Even if f″(0)=0, there are examples where the signs are the same.
y-m-67-07.s.s1.r.c: You read the rows where f″=0 and the signs on both sides are the same as counterexamples.
y-m-67-07.s.s1.explain: For n=4 and 6, f″ is positive on both sides of 0, so the curve does not change between concave and convex. A single counterexample breaks "always."
y-m-67-07.s.s2.prompt: For f(x) = xⁿ, find and enter 3 different values of n for which f″(0)=0 but (0, 0) is not an inflection point. (n is a natural number that is at least 3, and an n not in the table is fine too.)
y-m-67-07.s.s2.hint.0: Look at what property of n can separate the difference between the rows n=4, 6 and the rows n=3, 5 in the table.
y-m-67-07.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a candidate n and calculate the signs of f″(−1) and f″(1) yourself to check whether they are the same.
y-m-67-07.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number that is at least 3.
y-m-67-07.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number that is at least 3.
y-m-67-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The sign of f″ is the same on both sides of 0.
y-m-67-07.s.s2.fail.c2: For this n, the sign of f″ differs on the two sides of 0, so (0, 0) is an inflection point.
y-m-67-07.s.s2.explain: In f″(x) = n(n−1)xⁿ⁻², if n is even then n−2 is also even, so f″ is positive even when x is negative. So the signs on both sides of 0 are the same. If n is odd, the sign changes and it is an inflection point.
y-m-67-07.s.s3.prompt: Write for Dohyun, in one or two sentences, what you need to check besides f″(a)=0 in order to say that (a, f(a)) is an inflection point.
y-m-67-07.s.s3.hint.0: Describe in words the graph of f″ when n=3 and when n=4 (what sign is it to the left of 0, and to the right?).
y-m-67-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare what the necessary condition and the sufficient condition are with Dohyun's sentence.
y-m-67-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write so that it shows that "f″=0" is only a necessary condition and is not sufficient?
y-m-67-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tie it to the example you gave (x⁴ and so on)?
y-m-67-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say where on both sides of the point to look (for example, to the left and the right of a)?
y-m-67-07.s.s3.model.0: f″(a)=0 alone is not enough. You have to check that the sign of f″ on the two sides of that point changes from positive to negative, or from negative to positive, for it to be an inflection point.
y-m-67-07.s.s3.model.1: You have to check whether, before and after the point where f″=0, the curve is concave and then convex or the other way round. If both sides keep curving upward like x⁴, it is not an inflection point.

y-m-67-08.title: An integral whose value came out strangely small after substitution
y-m-67-08.topic: Integration methods: integration by substitution (definite integrals)
y-m-67-08.goal: Learn that when you change the variable in a definite integral you must also change the interval of integration, and write a piece for a friend explaining how to check the size of a result by estimation.
y-m-67-08.material: Yuna found the value of the definite integral ∫₀¹ 2x(x²+1)³ dx (read as: the integral from 0 to 1 of 2x times (x squared plus 1) cubed, with respect to x) using substitution. The integrand 2x(x²+1)³ of this integral is at least 0 for 0≤x≤1, and it is 0 at x=0 and 16 at x=1.
y-m-67-08.thinking.0: Find the error line in the solution
y-m-67-08.thinking.2: Check yourself by estimating the size
y-m-67-08.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-08.prereq.2: Differentiating a composite function (the basis of integration by substitution)
y-m-67-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Yuna's solution.
y-m-67-08.s.s1.hint.0: Using the fact that the integrand is 0 at x=0 and 16 at x=1, estimate whether 1/4 is a plausible size.
y-m-67-08.s.s1.hint.1: When line 2 changes dx to du, check which variable's values the numbers written at the lower and upper limits are.
y-m-67-08.s.s1.line.0: Letting u = x² + 1, we get du = 2x dx.
y-m-67-08.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the value we want is 1/4.
y-m-67-08.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. When you change the variable from x to u, the interval of integration must also be changed to values of u, but the interval 0, 1 for x was used as it was. The calculation in line 3 is right for that interval, but it is not the value the problem asks for, so line 4 is wrong.
y-m-67-08.s.s2.prompt: Which is the correct expression, fixed while still using Yuna's substitution u = x² + 1?
y-m-67-08.s.s2.hint.0: Put x=0 and x=1 into u = x² + 1 each.
y-m-67-08.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the value calculated on the new interval with the size you first estimated.
y-m-67-08.s.s2.r.a: The interval is still the values of x. When the variable changes, the same point becomes a different number.
y-m-67-08.s.s2.r.b: This calculated the values of u that correspond to both x=0 and x=1 and changed the interval.
y-m-67-08.s.s2.r.c: This changed only the upper limit to a value of u and left the lower limit as it was.
y-m-67-08.s.s2.r.d: 2x was already absorbed by du=2x dx, but x remained again, so the two variables got mixed.
y-m-67-08.s.s2.explain: When x=0, u=1, and when x=1, u=2. ∫₁² u³ du = [u⁴/4]₁² = 16/4 − 1/4 = 15/4, and since the integrand grows up to 16, 15/4 (=3.75) is far more plausible than 1/4.
y-m-67-08.s.s3.prompt: Write a message to send to Yuna. Include where and how it went wrong, the correct value, and one way of checking that she can use to catch errors by herself from now on.
y-m-67-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write what Yuna did and what needs to be fixed in one sentence each.
y-m-67-08.s.s3.hint.1: Among the ways of finding out whether a calculated value is right, choose one that you can try right away on this problem.
y-m-67-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you point to where Yuna went wrong by line number or by expression?
y-m-67-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Along with the correct value, did you give the reason why it comes out that way?
y-m-67-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is the checking method one that can be used not only for this problem but also for other substitution problems?
y-m-67-08.s.s3.model.0: Yuna, in line 2 you changed the variable to u, but you left the interval as 0 and 1, which are values of x. When x=0, u=1, and when x=1, u=2, so you should write ∫₁² u³du. Then it is 15/4. As a way to check, since the integrand is 16 at x=1, you can estimate that 1/4 is too small.
y-m-67-08.s.s3.model.1: When you substitute, you have to change the upper and lower limits to values of u as well. Since u=x²+1, the interval becomes 1 to 2. Then it is (16−1)/4, that is, 3.75. Or you can turn it back into x and check that putting 0 and 1 into (x²+1)⁴/4 gives the same value.

y-m-67-09.title: ∫ x ln x dx solved by two methods
y-m-67-09.topic: Integration methods: comparing two methods of integration by parts
y-m-67-09.goal: Confirm that the length of the calculation can differ depending on how you choose u and v′ in integration by parts, and that even a method that looks like a failure gives the same result once simplified, and write the reason for your choice.
y-m-67-09.material: Two students try to find the indefinite integral ∫ x ln x dx (x>0; read as: the integral of x times the natural logarithm of x, with respect to x) by integration by parts, ∫u v′ dx = uv − ∫u′ v dx. Jihu lets u = ln x and v′ = x, and Haeun lets u = x and v′ = ln x. (Suppose you already know that the indefinite integral of ln x is x ln x − x. The constant of integration is written as C.)
y-m-67-09.thinking.0: Predict how good each method is
y-m-67-09.thinking.1: Compare the prediction with the actual calculation
y-m-67-09.thinking.2: Explain the reason for a choice with grounds
y-m-67-09.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-09.prereq.1: The integration by parts formula ∫u v′ dx = uv − ∫u′ v dx
y-m-67-09.s.s1.prompt: Before starting to calculate, which is the most fitting prediction about the two methods?
y-m-67-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write u′ and v for each of the two ways and compare which is simpler.
y-m-67-09.s.s1.hint.1: For Haeun's way, write what you have to integrate to find v.
y-m-67-09.s.s1.o.a: Jihu's way looks easier. Differentiating ln x gives the simple 1/x.
y-m-67-09.s.s1.r.a: You compared the cost of finding u′ and v together.
y-m-67-09.s.s1.o.b: Haeun's way is easier. This is because differentiating u = x gives the constant 1.
y-m-67-09.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the side where u′ is simple and did not consider the work needed to find v (integrating ln x).
y-m-67-09.s.s1.o.c: I cannot decide which of the two ways is easier before calculating.
y-m-67-09.s.s1.r.c: This puts off judging before trying. You may put it off, but to compare you have to form a prediction.
y-m-67-09.s.s1.explain: You can predict that Jihu's choice will be short, since differentiating u makes it simple (1/x) and v′=x can be integrated right away. But this does not mean that Haeun's choice is impossible.
y-m-67-09.s.s1.acc.0: It is possible to put off judging before calculating, but forming a prediction and checking it by calculation helps the comparison.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.prompt: Haeun calculated with u = x and v = x ln x − x, and got I = ∫ x ln x dx = x(x ln x − x) − ∫(x ln x − x) dx = x² ln x − x² − I + x²/2. I appears again on the right side. What happens to this method?
y-m-67-09.s.s2.hint.0: Try treating I as the unknown and see whether you can rearrange the equation with I on both sides.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.hint.1: Differentiate the result you got and check whether it comes back to x ln x.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.o.a: I appears again, so this method cannot solve it.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.r.a: This treated the same integral appearing again as an immediate failure. Check whether you can see the whole expression as an equation in I.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.o.b: I appeared again, so it is a calculation mistake and I have to start over.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.r.b: I appearing again and a calculation mistake are different. You asserted a mistake without checking whether the earlier lines are right.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.o.c: If you rearrange it as an equation in I, you get the same result as Jihu.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.r.c: You saw the expression with I on both sides as a single equation.
y-m-67-09.s.s2.explain: Setting x² ln x − x²/2 − I equal to I gives 2I = x² ln x − x²/2, so I = (x²/2) ln x − x²/4 + C. Jihu's result is the same. Differentiating the expression you found gives x ln x.
y-m-67-09.s.s3.prompt: Choose which method you would use on this problem, and write how the results of the two methods are the same (or different) and your reason for choosing it.
y-m-67-09.s.s3.hint.0: Write the final expressions of the two methods side by side and compare whether they are equal.

y-m-67-10.topic: Integration methods: the value of a definite integral and distance traveled
y-m-67-10.goal: Learn the difference between the value of a definite integral (displacement) and area or distance traveled, and make and explain an example yourself in which the displacement is 0 but the distance traveled is positive.
y-m-67-10.material: Let v(t) m/s be the velocity at time t (seconds) of a robot moving along a straight line. Take the rightward direction as +, and let v(t) be continuous. (Displacement is the change in position from the first position to the later position, and distance traveled is the sum of all the lengths run regardless of direction.) Below is an attempt to find the "total distance traveled" when v(t) = t − 2, 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.
y-m-67-10.thinking.1: Decide whether the information is sufficient
y-m-67-10.thinking.2: Make examples that meet the condition
y-m-67-10.prereq.0: It is assumed that you have already learned limits of functions and derivatives of polynomial functions at the Calculus I level. The "H2" in this task is only a difficulty label assigned for production and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade.
y-m-67-10.prereq.2: The meaning of velocity, displacement, and distance traveled (the relationship between velocity and position covered in Calculus I)
y-m-67-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in the solution below. (The cause line is best, but the conclusion line is also accepted.)
y-m-67-10.s.s1.hint.0: Look at what the sign of v(t) = t − 2 is at t=0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
y-m-67-10.s.s1.hint.1: Say whether the robot is going right or left at t=1.
y-m-67-10.s.s1.line.0: The total distance traveled is the value of the velocity v(t) integrated from 0 to 4.
y-m-67-10.s.s1.line.2: Therefore the total distance traveled is 0 m.
y-m-67-10.s.s1.line.3: That is, the robot did not move even once during the 4 seconds.
y-m-67-10.s.s1.explain: Line 1 is the root cause. ∫v dt is the change in position (the displacement), and the total distance traveled is the sum of the lengths run regardless of direction. The calculation in line 2 correctly shows that the displacement is 0 m. Lines 3 and 4 are conclusions that wrongly read a displacement of 0 as a distance traveled of 0.
y-m-67-10.s.s2.prompt: For another robot, all we are told is that "the displacement from 0 seconds to b seconds is 0" (the velocity is continuous). What can you say about the total distance traveled?
y-m-67-10.s.s2.hint.0: Think of two different motions with a displacement of 0 (one of them being staying still).
y-m-67-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the total distance traveled in each motion.
y-m-67-10.s.s2.o.c: It is twice the displacement. This is because going and coming back doubles the distance.
y-m-67-10.s.s2.r.c: You wrote the relationship between the length of the round trip and the displacement wrongly. If the displacement is 0, twice it is also 0.
y-m-67-10.s.s2.explain: Even if the displacement is 0, the distance traveled can be 0 (stopped from beginning to end) or positive. You need the velocity formula or the times when the sign changes.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.prompt: There is a robot with velocity v(t) = t − c (c>0). Choose 3 different pairs (c, b) for which the displacement from 0 seconds to b seconds is 0. (c and b are positive; decimals are fine.)
y-m-67-10.s.s3.hint.0: Integrate the displacement directly at c=1 and c=2 and find the rule for b being how many times c when it becomes 0.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.hint.1: Using the time t=c when v becomes 0 as the boundary, calculate the displacement of the earlier interval and the later interval separately.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.ok.c1: c and b are both positive.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.fail.c1: c and b must be greater than 0.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.fail.c2: The displacement from 0 seconds to b seconds is not 0.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.explain: The displacement ∫₀ᵇ (t−c) dt = b²/2 − cb = b(b−2c)/2, so it is 0 when b=2c. The distance traveled then is ∫₀^(2c) |t−c| dt = c², and since c>0 it is always greater than 0.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.because.prompt: Choose one of the (c, b) you made, write why the displacement is 0 but the total distance traveled is not 0, and find the total distance traveled (m) in that case.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write the length the robot went in each of the two intervals as a positive number and add them.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.because.hint.1: First find the time when the velocity is 0 in the example you chose.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain from the viewpoint of direction why a displacement of 0 and a distance traveled of 0 are different?
y-m-67-10.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: In the distance traveled calculation, did you add the length of the negative interval as a positive number?
y-m-67-10.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you calculate the distance yourself with the (c, b) I chose?
y-m-67-10.s.s3.because.model.0: If c=2 and b=4, for the first 2 seconds the velocity is negative, so it goes 2 m to the left, and for the last 2 seconds the velocity is positive, so it comes 2 m to the right, so the displacement is 0. But the total distance traveled is 2+2=4 m.
y-m-67-10.s.s3.because.model.1: If c=1 and b=2, during the first 1 second the sign of the velocity is negative, so it goes back 1/2 m, and in the next 1 second it comes forward 1/2 m and returns to where it started. The total distance traveled is 1/2+1/2=1 m, that is, c².
y-m-67-10.title: Finding a Robot's Distance Traveled from Its Velocity
y-m-67-10.s.s2.o.a: It is 0 m. This is because the position did not change.
y-m-67-10.s.s2.r.a: The initial and final positions being the same is a different matter from not moving along the way.
y-m-67-10.s.s2.o.b: It cannot be determined. Even if the displacement is 0, we need to know more about how it moved along the way.
y-m-67-10.s.s2.r.b: You saw that displacement alone cannot tell us about the movement along the way.
